### Suggestions and fixes

An editor suggestion writes the prop in the class's place where that is certain: the prop's value puts this one class on the part and nothing else (no class the part makes from several props reads it), the class has no variant and is written once in a plain `className` string on the element itself, and the element neither sets that prop nor spreads props. The suggestion renders the same. Nothing runs under `--fix`: dropping a class changes what renders, which is the author's decision.

### Allowances

The rule is off in the package preset, so the kit keeps no allowance for it. The application's list, `scripts/lint-allow.json`, has no entry for it, and `scripts/check-allow-lists.mjs` rejects a new one. A comment that turns the rule off is reported by [`ledger/no-inline-config`](#ledgerno-inline-config), except a line or next-line disable that names it and says why after `--`; those are counted and may only shrink too.

### Limits

- It runs on product code only, never on the kit's own source, where patterns compose components by design.
- A class another Ledger rule reports is that rule's alone: a class rule's (a margin, a palette colour, an unknown variant), the padding, gap, display and grid template `ledger/use-primitives` judges on a layout primitive, and the type and neutral colour `ledger/cell-plain` judges on a `Table.Cell`.
- A focus target (a literal `tabIndex={-1}`) may carry `outline-none`, `outline-hidden` and `outline-focused`. A class a part's `@accepts` contract takes passes, whatever the part sets.
- What a part sets is what the build could read in its source; where it stopped (`unread` in parts.json), the part may set more than the rule knows. What it makes from several props counts with none of them written only where the build can tell the value then: a default, a known test, a helper's `if`s and returns; a value it cannot follow counts only where one of the props is written. A prop with a value of its own counts as set whether or not the element writes it. A class in no category is not judged.
- The classes are read as the class rules read them: through a condition, a template, a helper, a same-file `const` or map, and a spread that sets `className`. One passed in through a prop, imported from another file or built at runtime is not seen (`ledger/readable-classes` reports it on a kit part).
- A class that styles the inside of an element is reported where a kit part is written inside it in the same file, or where the element is one; a part another component renders there, or `children` handed in, is not seen. A kit component's inside may hold any tag, so a tag selector (`[&_p]:`) that reaches one is reported even where the component draws no such tag; a layout or type primitive's own element is matched by the tag it renders. A variant that reaches a sibling (`[&+div]:`) is not judged.
- A cell is a `cell` renderer handed to a column builder (the parameter of the function `defineColumns` takes, or one typed `ColumnKinds`), or a `Table.Cell` or `Table.Tree` around the element. A renderer passed by name is not followed.

## ledger/use-heading

Reports a raw `h1` to `h6` that carries type classes, which copy a title's look by hand.

### Reports

- An `h1` to `h6` whose `className` carries a type class, under any variant: a type style (`font-heading-page`, `font-body`, `font-code`), a weight (`font-semibold`, `font-bold`), a size (`text-xl`, `text-[20px]`), a line height (`leading-tight`) or a tracking (`tracking-tight`). The finding lists the type classes and names the Heading size they match: `<h2> carries type classes ("font-heading-page"), which copy a title's look by hand. Write <Heading size="page" as="h2">, or the kit part that draws this title (PageHeader.Title, Section.Title, DialogTitle).`
- The size comes from the classes: `font-heading-page` is `page`, `font-heading-section` or `font-body` at `font-semibold` is `section`, `font-heading-overlay` is `overlay` and `font-heading-display` is `display`; the earlier steps name the size that replaced them (`font-heading-xsmall` is `overlay`, `font-heading-large` is `display`, `font-heading-medium` is `page`, and `font-heading-small` is `page` at `font-semibold`). Classes that match no size (`text-xl font-bold`) name the four sizes to choose from.
- An `h1` to `h6` in the `render` of a kit part that sets its own type, such as DialogTitle or Section.Title: `<h3> in DialogTitle's render carries type classes ("font-heading-overlay"), which change the type DialogTitle sets for its title. Render the bare element, render={<h3 />}, and let the part draw the type.`

A class that is not type passes: layout, colour, `sr-only`, and `outline-none` on a focus target. The classes are read as the class rules read them, through a condition, a template, a class helper, a same-file `const` or map, and a spread that sets `className`.

### Why

A title in the kit is one of four sizes, each the title of a part: `page` is PageHeader.Title's, `section` Section.Title's, `overlay` the title of a Dialog, Sheet, AlertDialog or Drawer, and `display` the one size above them. Those parts render a Heading, so a title set with Heading matches the screen it sits in and follows the ramp when it changes ([Heading](?path=/docs/primitives-heading--docs)). Type classes on a raw heading copy one of those looks, or invent a fifth, and drift from the ramp the next time it changes: the record title that is 22px on one screen and 20px on the next. The element is the page's outline, chosen by the page; the size is the design's, chosen by the title it matches.

### Instead

- A title the kit draws: `PageHeader.Title` for the page or record, `Section.Title` for a section, `DialogTitle` (or `SheetTitle`, `AlertDialogTitle`, `DrawerTitle`) for an overlay.
- Any other title: `<Heading size="page" as="h2">`, at the size it matches, with `as` for the level the outline needs.
- A part's title at another level: `render={<h3 />}`, bare; the part keeps its type.
- A heading that only the outline needs, such as a focus target or one read by a screen reader alone, carries no type classes: `<h2 tabIndex={-1} className="sr-only outline-none">`.

### Examples

#### Reported

```tsx reported
export function RecordTitle({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return <h1 className="font-heading-page">{name}</h1>;
}
```

```tsx reported
import { Stack, Text } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function GroupTitle({ title, count }: { title: string; count: number }) {
  return (
    <Stack space="space.050">
      <h3 className="font-body font-semibold">{title}</h3>
      <Text>{count} records</Text>
    </Stack>
  );
}
```

```tsx reported
import { DialogTitle } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function RemoveTitle() {
  return (
    <DialogTitle render={<h2 className="font-heading-page" />}>Remove this allocation?</DialogTitle>
  );
}
```

#### Allowed

```tsx allowed
import { Heading } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function RecordTitle({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return (
    <Heading size="page" as="h1">
      {name}
    </Heading>
  );
}
```

```tsx allowed
import { DialogTitle } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function RemoveTitle() {
  return <DialogTitle render={<h3 />}>Remove this allocation?</DialogTitle>;
}
```

```tsx allowed
export function StepHeading({ title }: { title: string }) {
  return (
    <h2 tabIndex={-1} className="sr-only outline-none">
      {title}
    </h2>
  );
}
```

### Suggestions and fixes

The rule offers no `--fix`: the element changes, and the size is a design decision the author confirms. It offers an editor suggestion where the `className` is one plain string and the file can name Heading (it imports the kit's Heading, the kit as a namespace, or other parts by name, to which the suggestion adds Heading), and the heading sets no `style`, which Heading does not take:

- A raw heading whose classes match a size becomes a Heading of that size and level, without its type classes and keeping the rest: `<h2 className="font-heading-page text-subtle">` becomes `<Heading size="page" as="h2" className="text-subtle">`.
- A heading in a part's `render` drops its type classes: `render={<h2 className="font-heading-page" />}` becomes `render={<h2 />}`.

Classes that match no size get no suggestion.

### Allowances

The rule takes the plugin's `allow` option: a count of reports per file that may only shrink. It is in the recommended preset as an error and not in the package preset, since the kit's parts draw their titles from their own classes. Neither the kit's `test/lint-allow.json` nor the application's `scripts/lint-allow.json` has an entry for it. A comment that turns the rule off, a block disable, or a line disable with no reason after `--` is reported by [`ledger/no-inline-config`](#ledgerno-inline-config).

### Limits

- It reads the elements by their tag, `h1` to `h6`; a component that renders a heading, or a heading created with `createElement`, is not checked.
- A class passed in through a prop, imported from another file or built at runtime is not seen.
- A heading in the `render` of a kit part that sets no type of its own, or of a component that is not the kit's, is read as a raw heading.
- A Heading with type classes is [`ledger/no-restyle`](#ledgerno-restyle)'s, which reports a class that changes the type its `size` sets.

## ledger/use-primitives

Reports layout written as classes: on a plain element, where a primitive belongs, and on a primitive, where its props belong.

### Reports

- A plain `div`, `span`, `section`, `article`, `aside`, `header`, `footer`, `main`, `nav`, `ul`, `ol`, `li`, `form`, `fieldset`, `p`, `label` or `h1` to `h6` whose `className` has a display class (`flex`, `inline-flex`, `grid`, `inline-grid`) or a padding or gap class (`p-`, `px-`, `py-`, `pt-`, `pb-`, `ps-`, `pe-`, `gap-`), with no variant. The finding lists the layout classes and names, in one sentence, the part they make with its props and their token values: `<div> carries layout classes (flex, gap-100). Use <Inline space="space.100">.`
- A Box, Stack, Inline, Flex or Grid from the kit whose `className` sets what one of its props sets: padding, a gap, its display, or grid columns and rows. The finding lists the classes and says, in one sentence, what to write instead: `<Stack> carries layout classes (p-200, gap-100). Use space="space.100" and wrap it in <Box padding="space.200"> (a Stack has no padding).`
- The same through a component of the file that hands its `className` on to a primitive (`const Pane = (props) => <Stack {...props} />`), at each `<Pane className="…">`: `<Pane> forwards className to <Stack>, which then carries layout classes (pt-200). For the <Stack> inside <Pane>: wrap it in <Box paddingBlockStart="space.200"> (a Stack has no padding).` The props are the Stack's, which `Pane` need not take: give it one that hands them on, or change the Stack inside it.

The part and its props are computed from the classes:

- The part: a grid display or a grid template is a Grid, a flex display with `flex-col` a Stack and without it an Inline, a gap alone a Stack (an Inline for a column gap alone), and padding alone a Box. On a primitive that is already the part, a display it has already is dropped (`Drop flex (an Inline is already a flex row).`); a Box that lays out its children puts them in the part inside it.
- Padding: Box's `padding`, `paddingInline`, `paddingBlock` or one side (`paddingBlockStart` for `pt-`); on another primitive, a Box around it.
- A gap: `space` on Stack, `space` and `rowSpace` on Inline, `gap`, `columnGap` or `rowGap` on Flex and Grid.
- Grid columns and rows: Grid's `templateColumns`, one template per window breakpoint (`templateColumns={{ md: "repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))" }}`), and `templateRows`. It keys only `base`, `sm`, `md`, `lg` and `xl`, so a column class under any other variant (a Ledger breakpoint such as `aside:`, a state) names `templateColumns` and says so, with no object. A Stack's `space` is its row gap: a column gap on a Stack is dropped (`a Stack has no column gap`), and where a gap and an axis gap are both written, the axis gap sets its prop. A plain element's `gap-px` alone is on no space step, and the finding says to give a part a space token or draw the hairline with a border or a Separator.
- A value: a Ledger space key is its token (`gap-100` is `space="space.100"`); a stock step or an arbitrary length is the step it equals, or the one nearest it, which the finding says (`paddingInline="space.150" (nearest 13px)`); a value the lint cannot read is `space.…`.

On a primitive, a class under a container query (`@3xl:`) is not reported, nor a padding, gap or display class under any other variant (`md:px-300`, `hidden md:flex`), nor `gap-px`. Grid columns are not reported when any column or row class on the element is under a container query, since `templateColumns` follows the window and cannot say that. The part is recognised through an alias or a namespace import from the kit, and a local component, another package's part or a parameter that shares a primitive's name is not checked. An element whose `render` puts a primitive in its place (`<Slot render={<Stack />} className="pt-200">`) gives the primitive its classes, and the finding says so: `<Slot> renders <Stack>, which then carries layout classes (pt-200). Wrap it in <Box paddingBlockStart="space.200"> (a Stack has no padding).`

`configs.recommended` sets the rule to warn, and `configs.package` leaves it off. This repository's root `eslint.config.js` raises it to an error for the application's files.

### Why

A primitive's layout is its props: each one is typed to a token, so a wrong value is a type error, and one prop changes a layout everywhere it is used. The same layout written as classes on a `div` or over a primitive's props is invisible to both: it takes any value, and it overrides the part without the part knowing. A component decides its inside and its parent decides the space around it, so rows and columns are Stack and Inline first, and Flex and Grid only for what those cannot express ([Primitives](?path=/docs/primitives-overview--docs)).

### Instead

The primitive for the layout, with its props in place of the classes: Stack, Inline, Box, Grid or Flex.

- A column: `<Stack space="space.200">`. A row: `<Inline space="space.100" alignBlock="center">`, with `shouldWrap` and `rowSpace` when it wraps, and `display="inline-flex"` beside text.
- Padding and a fill: `<Box padding="space.200" backgroundColor="elevation.surface.raised">`, or one side (`paddingBlockStart`).
- Columns: `<Grid templateColumns={{ base: "1fr", md: "repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))" }} gap="space.200">`. A grid inside a panel takes one intrinsic template, such as `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 144px), 1fr))`, or column classes under a container query.
- What Stack and Inline cannot express: `<Flex direction="row" gap="space.100" wrap="wrap">`.
- A layout no primitive can express is a kit change, made through `/ledger-add-part`.

### Examples

#### Reported

```tsx reported
import { Badge, Text } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function ProgramTitle({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return (
    <div className="flex items-center gap-100">
      <Text weight="semibold">{name}</Text>
      <Badge tone="warning">Draft</Badge>
    </div>
  );
}
```

```tsx reported
import { Stack, Text } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function Summary() {
  return (
    <Stack className="p-200 gap-100">
      <Text>Three requirements have no evidence.</Text>
      <Text>Upload it before the assessment on Friday.</Text>
    </Stack>
  );
}
```

```tsx reported
import { Grid, Text } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function BoardColumns() {
  return (
    <Grid className="grid-cols-3 gap-200">
      <Text>Open</Text>
      <Text>In review</Text>
      <Text>Done</Text>
    </Grid>
  );
}
```

```tsx reported
import { Stack, type StackProps } from "@ledger/design-system";

// A component of the file that hands its className on to a Stack.
const Pane = (props: StackProps) => <Stack {...props} />;

export function Notes() {
  return <Pane className="pt-200">Three requirements have no evidence.</Pane>;
}
```

#### Allowed

```tsx allowed
import { Badge, Inline, Text } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function ProgramTitle({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return (
    <Inline space="space.100" alignBlock="center">
      <Text weight="semibold">{name}</Text>
      <Badge tone="warning">Draft</Badge>
    </Inline>
  );
}
```

```tsx allowed
import { Box, Stack, Text } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function Summary() {
  return (
    <Box padding="space.200">
      <Stack space="space.100">
        <Text>Three requirements have no evidence.</Text>
        <Text>Upload it before the assessment on Friday.</Text>
      </Stack>
    </Box>
  );
}
```

```tsx allowed

  return (
    <Grid templateColumns={{ base: "1fr", md: "repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))" }} gap="space.200">
      <Text>Open</Text>
      <Text>In review</Text>
      <Text>Done</Text>
    </Grid>
  );
}
```

```tsx allowed

  return (
    <Box className="@container">
      <Grid gap="space.200" className="grid-cols-1 @3xl:grid-cols-3">
        <Text>Open</Text>
        <Text>In review</Text>
        <Text>Done</Text>
      </Grid>
    </Box>
  );

```

### Suggestions and fixes

Neither. Moving a layout from classes to a primitive or its props changes the element, and sometimes adds one (a Box around a Stack for its padding), so the rule offers no `--fix` and no editor suggestion.

### Allowances

The rule takes the plugin's `allow` option: a count of reports per file that may only shrink. A file with more reports than its count fails, and one with fewer fails until the count is lowered. The rule is off in `configs.package`. This repository's `scripts/lint-allow.json` has no entry for it, so every report in the application fails. A comment that turns the rule off, a block disable, or a line disable with no reason after `--` is reported by [`ledger/no-inline-config`](#ledgerno-inline-config).

### Limits

- It reads the classes that reach `className` as the class rules read them: through a condition, a template, a class helper, a same-file `const` or map entry, and an object spread onto the element that sets `className` and is not written over by a later one (JSX keeps the last); a class passed in through a prop or imported from another file is not seen.
- A component that hands its `className` on to a primitive is followed within the file, through up to four such components, when its first parameter carries it: the props object or a rest that still holds it, spread onto the element, or `className` destructured (in the parameter, or from the props object at the top of its body) and written onto it. Of the elements a component hands it to, the first in source order counts, passing over one that renders a component already on the way (a tree that renders itself). A component imported from another file, one declared with `let`, one read from an object (`<parts.Row>`), a component past the fourth and a second element given the same prop are not followed.
- On a plain element, a class under a variant (`md:flex`, `md:p-200`) is not reported, nor the physical padding sides `pl-` and `pr-`, nor an element outside the list above, such as `button`, `dl` or `table`.
- On a primitive, only padding, gap, display and grid template classes are read; the other layout classes (alignment, position, size) are left to the part's props or to the classes as written.

## ledger/product-responsive-table

Reports a kit DataTable that turns `responsive` off, or leaves it to a prop spread.

### Reports

- A `DataTable` whose last `responsive` is not the literal `true`: `responsive={false}`, a string, or an expression the rule cannot read. The finding says how the prop is written: `<DataTable> sets responsive={false}, so a narrow frame scrolls it sideways instead of folding lower-priority columns into More fields. A DataTable is responsive by default: remove the prop.`
- A `DataTable` with a prop spread after its last `responsive`, or with a spread and no `responsive`, since the spread can turn it off: `<DataTable> leaves responsive to a prop spread, which can turn it off and scroll the table sideways instead of folding lower-priority columns into More fields. Write responsive after the spread.`

A `DataTable` that leaves the prop out passes: it is responsive by default. Only a `DataTable` imported from `@ledger/design-system` is checked, through an alias or a namespace import too; a local component of the same name, or a type import, is not.

### Why

A product register has to fit the space it is given: beside an open preview panel, in a narrow window, on a phone. A responsive DataTable measures its container and keeps the record's name and the row actions, moving lower-priority fields into each row's More fields ("+3"), so no field disappears and no table scrolls sideways. `responsive={false}` makes it scroll instead, which hides columns without saying so. Every product DataTable is responsive: the product patterns' Registers section is the contract (product patterns (`docs/guides/product-patterns.md`)), and the Data table page describes the responsive mode ([Data table](?path=/docs/patterns-data-table--docs)).

### Instead

Leave `responsive` out: `<DataTable table={table} />`. Behind a prop spread, write `responsive` after it: `<DataTable {...props} responsive />`. Give the name column `priority: 0` and a readable width in `defineColumns`, so the name stays in the row when the rest fold.

### Examples

#### Reported

```tsx reported
import { DataTable, defineColumns, useDataTable } from "@ledger/design-system";

type Risk = { id: string; title: string; status: string };

const columns = defineColumns<Risk>((c) => [c.text("title", { header: "Risk", priority: 0 })]);

export function RiskTable({ risks }: { risks: Risk[] }) {
  const table = useDataTable({ columns, data: risks });
  return <DataTable table={table} responsive={false} />;
}
```

```tsx reported
import type { ComponentProps } from "react";
import { DataTable } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function RegisterTable(props: ComponentProps<typeof DataTable>) {
  return <DataTable responsive {...props} />;
}
```

#### Allowed

```tsx allowed
import { DataTable, defineColumns, useDataTable } from "@ledger/design-system";

type Risk = { id: string; title: string; status: string };

const columns = defineColumns<Risk>((c) => [c.text("title", { header: "Risk", priority: 0 })]);

export function RiskTable({ risks }: { risks: Risk[] }) {
  const table = useDataTable({ columns, data: risks });
  return <DataTable table={table} />;
}
```

```tsx allowed
import type { ComponentProps } from "react";
import { DataTable } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function RegisterTable(props: ComponentProps<typeof DataTable>) {
  return <DataTable {...props} responsive />;
}
```

### Suggestions and fixes

Neither. The rule offers no `--fix` and no editor suggestion: a table made responsive again also needs its column priorities and widths chosen, which only the author can do.

### Allowances

The rule is in neither preset: a horizontally scrolling comparison table (`responsive={false}`) remains a supported kit use, so a product turns it on for the files that follow its contract. This repository's root `eslint.config.js` turns it on, as an error, for the application's product files (`src/routes`, `src/components/app`, `src/components/prototype`, `src/lib` and `src/router.tsx`). It takes the plugin's `allow` option, a count of reports per file that may only shrink; `scripts/lint-allow.json` has no entry for it, so every report fails. A comment that turns the rule off, a block disable, or a line disable with no reason after `--` is reported by [`ledger/no-inline-config`](#ledgerno-inline-config).

### Limits

- A `responsive` that comes from an expression (`responsive={wide}`) is reported, since the rule cannot read its value.
- A spread is reported whatever it holds, since the rule cannot read it: write `responsive` after it.
- A wrapper component that renders the kit's `DataTable` is checked where it renders it, not where it is used.
- It does not check the columns: a name column without `priority: 0` or a readable width still passes.

## ledger/product-line-tabs

Reports a kit TabsList without `variant="line"` after any prop spread, or one given a class or style that changes how its strip wraps, sizes or scrolls.

### Reports

- A `TabsList` whose last `variant` is not the literal `"line"`, or is followed by a prop spread that could replace it. The finding says how the variant is written (`takes the default variant`, `sets variant="default"`, `leaves variant to a prop spread`): `<TabsList> takes the default variant. Product tabs are the line variant, whose underline spans the content width: write variant="line" after any prop spreads.`
- A `TabsList` whose `className` carries `flex-wrap`, `flex-wrap-reverse`, `w-fit`, `min-w-fit`, `max-w-fit` or any `overflow-*`, `overflow-x-*` or `overflow-y-*` class, also under a variant or with `!`: `"flex-wrap" on <TabsList> changes how the tab strip wraps, sizes or scrolls, which the kit owns: one row that scrolls, under a line across the content width. Drop it.`
- A `TabsList` whose inline `style` sets `overflow`, `overflowX` or `overflowY`, sets `flexWrap` to `wrap` or `wrap-reverse`, or sets `width`, `minWidth` or `maxWidth` to `fit-content`, with the same message leading with the property (`style.overflowX on <TabsList> …`).

One element can have both reports. Only a `TabsList` imported from `@ledger/design-system` is checked, through an alias or a namespace import too; a local component of the same name, or a type import, is not.

### Why

Every product page and preview uses the same tab strip: a line under the tabs that spans the content, a selected indicator that slides, and one row that scrolls when the labels do not fit, on a desktop preview and a phone alike. The kit owns that scroller, so a wrapping, fitted or hand-scrolled strip breaks the underline and the keyboard behaviour that come with it. The product patterns' Tabs section is the contract (product patterns (`docs/guides/product-patterns.md`)); the Tabs page describes both variants ([Tabs](?path=/docs/components-tabs--docs)).

### Instead

`<TabsList variant="line">`, after any prop spread, with no layout class or style. The kit spans the content and scrolls the strip in one row.

### Examples

#### Reported

```tsx reported
import { Tabs, TabsContent, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function ProgramTabs() {
  return (
    <Tabs defaultValue="overview">
      <TabsList>
        <TabsTrigger value="overview">Overview</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="systems">Systems</TabsTrigger>
      </TabsList>
      <TabsContent value="overview">Overview</TabsContent>
      <TabsContent value="systems">Systems</TabsContent>
    </Tabs>
  );
}
```

```tsx reported
import type { ComponentProps } from "react";
import { Tabs, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function RecordTabs(props: ComponentProps<typeof TabsList>) {
  return (
    <Tabs defaultValue="details">
      <TabsList variant="line" {...props}>
        <TabsTrigger value="details">Details</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="activity">Activity</TabsTrigger>
      </TabsList>
    </Tabs>
  );
}
```

```tsx reported
import { Tabs, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function EvidenceTabs() {
  return (
    <Tabs defaultValue="versions">
      <TabsList variant="line" className="flex-wrap">
        <TabsTrigger value="versions">Versions</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="links">Linked requirements</TabsTrigger>
      </TabsList>
    </Tabs>
  );
}
```

#### Allowed

```tsx allowed
import { Tabs, TabsContent, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function ProgramTabs() {
  return (
    <Tabs defaultValue="overview">
      <TabsList variant="line">
        <TabsTrigger value="overview">Overview</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="systems">Systems</TabsTrigger>
      </TabsList>
      <TabsContent value="overview">Overview</TabsContent>
      <TabsContent value="systems">Systems</TabsContent>
    </Tabs>
  );
}
```

```tsx allowed
import type { ComponentProps } from "react";
import { Tabs, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@ledger/design-system";

export function RecordTabs(props: ComponentProps<typeof TabsList>) {
  return (
    <Tabs defaultValue="details">
      <TabsList {...props} variant="line">
        <TabsTrigger value="details">Details</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="activity">Activity</TabsTrigger>
      </TabsList>
    </Tabs>
  );
}
```

### Suggestions and fixes

Neither. Adding or moving `variant="line"` and removing a class are small edits, but the rule does not make them: the rule offers no `--fix` and no editor suggestion.

### Allowances

The rule is in neither preset: filled tabs remain a supported kit variant, so a product turns it on for the files that follow its contract. This repository's root `eslint.config.js` turns it on, as an error, for the application's product files (`src/routes`, `src/components/app`, `src/components/prototype`, `src/lib` and `src/router.tsx`). It takes the plugin's `allow` option, a count of reports per file that may only shrink; `scripts/lint-allow.json` has no entry for it, so every report fails. A comment that turns the rule off, a block disable, or a line disable with no reason after `--` is reported by [`ledger/no-inline-config`](#ledgerno-inline-config).

### Limits

- A `variant` that comes from an expression (`variant={variant}`) is reported, since the rule cannot read its value; `variant={"line"}` passes.
- A wrapper component that renders the kit's `TabsList` is checked where it renders it, not where it is used, so props passed through the wrapper are not seen.
- Its classes are read as the class rules read them: through a condition, a template, a class helper, a same-file `const` or map entry, and an object spread onto the element that sets `className` and is not written over by a later one (JSX keeps the last). A `style` held in a variable, a class passed in through a prop or imported from another file, and a class or selector that reaches the strip from a parent (`[&_[role=tablist]]:flex-wrap`) are not read.

<!-- page: Guidance/Writing stories (src/stories/docs/Stories.mdx) -->

# Writing stories

The Storybook is the package's test suite and its documentation at once: every story renders in both colour modes with its play function and an axe pass (`npm run test:a11y`) and again at a phone and in a narrow frame (`npm run test:layout`), every exported part must appear in one (`npm run ds:check`), and the family's MDX page draws its examples from the same file. The MCP tool `get-storybook-story-instructions` is the generic Storybook guidance (the package runs Storybook 10); this page is what this package adds to it.

## Shape of a stories file

```tsx
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react-vite";
import { expect, fn, userEvent, within } from "storybook/test";

import { Badge, Button } from "../../components";
import { Inline, Stack } from "../../primitives";
import * as storyLayout from "../_lib/matrix";

// Story-only helpers, bound locally so the MCP snippet does not list them as package exports.
const { Matrix, Specimens } = storyLayout;

const meta = {
  title: "Components/Badge",
  component: Badge,
  parameters: { layout: "padded" },
  args: { children: "Featured", variant: "default" },
} satisfies Meta<typeof Badge>;
export default meta;
type Story = StoryObj<typeof meta>;

/** The usage to copy, first, with the controls. */
export const Playground: Story = {};

/** The six reference variants beside the icon positions. */
export const Variants: Story = {
  tags: ["!manifest"],
  render: () => <Matrix rows={…} cols={…} render={…} />,
};
```

- Imports come from `@storybook/react-vite` and `storybook/test`, never the `@storybook/test` or `@storybook/react` names.
- Parts are imported by relative path from `../../components`, `../../primitives`, `../../patterns`, `../../layout`. The package never imports its own root.
- `title` is `<Category>/<Family>`: Primitives, Components, Layout, Patterns, Tokens, Guidance. One family, one file, one `title`.
- The JSDoc comment above a story is its description on the docs page. Write it as the sentence the reader needs, not the story's name again.
- The first story in the manifest is the usage to copy: plain parts and primitives, no `_lib` helper, no element, component or function of the stories file, and no ref or storybook/test spy made at module level, alone or held in an object (`const refs = { nav: createRef() }`). A callback its play checks is an arg (`args: { onCopied: fn() }`, passed as `onCopied={args.onCopied}`), which the manifest prints in place as `fn()`. MCP `docs-show` returns the code of the first three stories Storybook's manifest holds, and an agent copies them. A family's comparison story may still lead its page, tagged out of the manifest (below), so the first story MCP returns is the first plain one. A story whose render is a component of the stories file shows in the manifest as that one call (`<LoadingDemo />`), with nothing to copy, so lead with a story that renders the parts themselves, such as the Playground, wherever the family has one. Where every story of a family is such a component, the first one's `render` is the component itself (`render: PickerStates`), and the manifest shows the component's body, so that body renders the parts directly too: a value accessor or a formatter is written inline (`value={(row, column) => …}`), not a function of the file. The second and third stories in the manifest are copied too: each may name a component of the stories file, as its one call or as a stand-in the reader replaces (a demo router link), but its own code names no ref, spy, function or element of the file. A callback its play checks is an `fn()` arg, a formatter or an accessor is written inline, and a check of refs and native attributes goes in a `NativeAttributes` story tagged `!manifest`. In all three, the manifest writes an arg in only where the code passes it straight to an element it returns, as `prop={args.key}` or `{...args}`, and then drops the `args` parameter: an arg read in a callback (`onSelect={() => args.onSelect("MS-A")}`), in an expression (`{args.invalid && …}`) or in JSX passed as a prop (`render={<Link onClick={args.onNavigate} />}`) stays `args.key` in a copy that has no `args`. Such a check goes in a story tagged `!manifest`, and a Playground whose code reads its controls that way is tagged `!manifest` too. `test/story-manifest.test.mjs` reads what the manifest prints (the story's render, a named render's body, the meta's render when the story has none, and the args they take) and every helper that code reaches.
- A `children` arg written as JSX in parentheses, as Prettier writes any JSX longer than a line, shows in the manifest with its parentheses as text (`<Alert>(<>…</>)</Alert>`). Write the children in the meta's `render` (`render: (args) => <Alert {...args}>…</Alert>`) and keep `args` for the props.
- `_lib` helpers (Matrix, Specimens, Pair) are story layout, not package exports. The MCP snippet lists every relative import under the package name, so a story file binds them locally (`import * as storyLayout from "../_lib/matrix"`, then `const { Matrix, Specimens } = storyLayout`); a locally declared name is left out of the snippet's import line.
- A story whose render shows a `_lib` helper (a Matrix or Specimens comparison), and every Don't, is tagged `!manifest`. It stays in the sidebar, on its page and in every test run, and leaves the manifest MCP reads, so `docs-show` never offers a comparison grid or a Don't as code to copy. A Don't an agent must know is also a sentence on the page (its Content, or a line under the Don't canvas), which `docs-show` returns under Docs. The token sheets are the exception: their stories are the Tokens pages' only examples, and they stay in the manifest with the sheet helpers bound locally.
- A deprecated part's stories leave the manifest together: its meta sets `tags: ["!manifest"]`, so MCP never offers the part as code to copy, while its page and its tests stay. A composition page whose stories are whole workspaces built from the file's own routes (Layout/Pages) does the same; its prose and the Recipes carry the composition.
- `!manifest` is the one tag a story sets. Storybook applies `dev`, `test` and `manifest` itself, and the layout checks measure every story, so no tag opts a story into a check.

## What to cover

- Every named part of the family, rendered. `ds:check` fails on an export with no story.
- Representative states, not every permutation: default, hover and pressed through the tokens, disabled, invalid, loading, empty, error, the sizes that change behaviour. The `_lib/matrix` **Matrix** and **Specimens** helpers lay a family's variants out for comparison.
- A Do beside a Don't wherever a misuse is likely: a wrong part (a Combobox for four values), a wrong word (a label that flips with the state, OK), a missing name (an unnamed group). **Pair** in `_lib/pair` lays them out with one line each on why. The story is tagged `!manifest`, and its `play` asserts what makes the Do right and the Don't wrong: the name, the role, the description or the state a reader meets. The family's page shows it under the section the misuse belongs to (When to use it, Content), beside a sentence that says the Don't. A family with no likely misuse has no pair; a pair is never filler.
- One playground covers the controls. Keep distinct regression cases as their own stories rather than folding them into the playground.
- A `play` function on every interactive story: drive it with `userEvent`, assert the visible outcome with role and label queries on `canvas`, and assert `fn` callbacks were called. Wait for a menu to mount before asserting `aria-expanded`.
- Render once. Josef switches the mode in the toolbar; a story never renders light and dark side by side.
- A story's frame is fluid: a wrapper takes `maxWidth`, not `width`, so it fits a phone and a panel. Inside a row that sizes its children to their content (Specimens, an Inline), give the width together with `maxWidth: "100%"`. A layout inside a story responds to its container (`@container` with `@md:`), not the window (`md:`). Set Frame to 320px container in the toolbar to see a story in a narrow container.
- A behaviour that exists only at a phone gets a story that pins `viewport` in its `globals` (`ledgerPhone` is 390px, `ledgerSmall` 340px), with a `play` that asserts it: no sideways scroll, the changed element visible, a folded item reachable. Pin only where the behaviour needs it: the layout checks measure a pinned story at the width it pins, not at theirs ([Testing and review](?path=/docs/guidance-testing-and-review--docs) says how).

  ```tsx
  export const Phone: Story = {
    globals: { viewport: { value: "ledgerPhone", isRotated: false } },
    play: async () => {
      const page = document.documentElement;
      await expect(page.scrollWidth).toBeLessThanOrEqual(page.clientWidth);
    },
  };
  ```

## What fails a story

- A console error, or a Base UI or React warning on `console.warn`. `test/storybook.setup.ts` fails any story that emits one.
- An axe violation in either mode. Fix semantic and structural violations directly; a contrast or spacing violation is a design decision, so raise it instead.
- Sideways scroll at a 390px phone, a word broken across two lines, or paint past a 320px frame (`npm run test:layout`). [Testing and review](?path=/docs/guidance-testing-and-review--docs) says what the check measures and when a story is exempt.
- A gate: a focus ring its container clips, a selected item that disappears in forced colours, a control under 24px or shown only on hover on a touch phone, an overlay control out of view in a short window, or long text that overflows (`npm run test:a11y` and `npm run test:gates`). A story that predates a gate is listed with its count in `test/gates-allow.json`, which may only shrink.
- A stale `api/public-api.json`: `npm run ds:api:check` when declarations changed, `ds:api:update` when they changed on purpose.
- Drift in `eslint-plugin/components.json` or `llms.txt`; the package build regenerates both.

## The MDX page

One `<Family>.mdx` beside the stories, attached with `<Meta of={Stories} />`, so its title is the stories file's. The first line under the title is the part's status: `**Status: Stable.**`, `**Status: Experimental.**` with why and who owns it, or `**Status: Deprecated.**` with what replaces it ([Upgrading](?path=/docs/guidance-upgrading--docs#status) says what each promises). A page that compares parts or describes a composition has none. Then the page says what the part is for in a sentence or two, then `<Canvas of={Stories.X} />` for the examples worth reading, `<ArgTypes of={Part} />` for each named part, and the usage and accessibility guidance that helps. No required heading set and no "Not applicable" filler. The page documents the current API; a deprecated spelling that still works gets at most one line naming its replacement. What an earlier spelling is written as now goes on [Upgrading](?path=/docs/guidance-upgrading--docs), under the family's name, and the page links it from Related.

`api/axis-policy.json` holds optional notes on package-specific meanings of `variant`, `size`, `tone` and the other shared axes; a new part or prop does not need an entry.

## What does not belong here

An application composition. A screen from the product is verified in the running app, never mounted in a package story; the package documents neutral contracts and the application's pattern contract decides how they are used there.

## After changing a story

Call `stories-changed`, then `stories-preview` for the stories that matter, then `test-run` for the family. Report the URLs. Add a `CHANGELOG.md` entry that names the story showing the change.

<!-- page: Guidance/Testing and review (src/stories/docs/TestingAndReview.mdx) -->

# Testing and review

The system should help a person understand the situation, choose an action, complete it, and recover if it fails. A familiar visual style alone does not establish that contract. Test the whole task with realistic content, keyboard input and the conditions people actually encounter.

## Before adding an API

Start with the user's task and the semantic HTML element. Reuse a native control when its behavior answers the task. A new prop needs a distinct consumer need and a documented default, valid combinations, ownership of state, and behavior when absent. Avoid booleans that encode several mutually exclusive modes. Prefer a union when only one mode can apply. Preserve native names for native behavior.

| Question                       | Required evidence                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Who owns the state?            | Controlled and uncontrolled behavior, defaults, reset, and async external updates.                         |
| What reaches the DOM?          | The target for `id`, `name`, `form`, `aria-*`, `data-*`, handlers, and the ref.                            |
| What can fail?                 | Pending, rejected save, retry, cancellation, and stale completion examples.                                |
| What can be composed?          | Compound slots and valid nesting; no interactive element inside another interactive element.               |
| What does a dependency expose? | Explicit adapter types for toast, table and chart APIs; all other implementation internals remain private. |

## State and content

Every collection needs loading, empty, filtered empty, error, ready, and refreshed states where applicable. A filtered empty state keeps filters visible and offers Clear filters. A save failure keeps the draft. Announce success only after the command succeeds; if persistence is local to this browser, say so. Permissions are business rules enforced by commands as well as reflected by controls.

Use sentence case, a specific verb for actions, and an error that says what the person can do next. Name the affected record when ambiguity is possible. Essential guidance belongs beside the control. Disabled actions need a visible reason; an enabled control must navigate or perform its stated action. Do not use a notification to conceal an unimplemented operation.

## Keyboard, focus and targets

Check Tab and Shift+Tab, Enter and Space, Escape, arrow keys, Home/End and typeahead where the widget requires them. Trees maintain one tab stop and expose level, expansion and selection. Closing a modal returns focus to its opener or an explicitly supplied replacement. Failed form submission focuses the first invalid control and exposes all errors. A sticky header or action bar must not fully obscure focused content.

The web minimum target requirement is **24 by 24 CSS pixels**, subject to the WCAG 2.2 spacing, equivalent, inline, user-agent and essential exceptions. Document any exception on the actual control. Native platform point guidance is not a CSS pixel requirement. Prefer larger targets for frequent touch actions. Measure both the target and the distance to neighboring targets; a small icon inside a sufficiently large button is fine.

Inspect 320 CSS pixel width, 200% text enlargement and 400% browser zoom. A dense data table may scroll in its own region; surrounding search, headings, dialogs and actions must reflow. Check focus after scrolling, opening menus, validating a long form, collapsing navigation, and removing the selected item. Reduced-motion preference should remove nonessential movement while keeping pending state understandable through text and semantics.

## Automated checks and their limits

`node scripts/ds-check.mjs` (`npm run ds:check`) resolves public exports through the TypeScript compiler, counts executable story references (a JSX element, a call, or a stories file's meta `component` when one of its stories renders from args), checks story coverage and that every family's stories have a page, and rejects a growing exception baseline. It fails when a compound's member is a function its module does not export (docgen documents a module's exports, so the member would get no props table) and when a family page renders no `<ArgTypes>` for its stories' component. It reports, without failing yet, the exported families with no page showing generated props, and how many catalog parts the application imports (`-- --usage` lists the rest). `node scripts/ds-public-api.mjs` prints the full public value/type inventory. A reference proves use, not correctness; interaction assertions establish behavior.

`test/api-conformance.test.mjs` (in `npm test`) reads every exported part through the TypeScript program and holds it to the component contract in the component library guide: every optional prop takes `undefined`; the caller's `className` and `ref` reach the element its other props land on; and `data-slot` comes after the caller's props, before them only on the base parts the guide names. A part that differs by design names its reason in the test's `EXCEPTIONS`. `test/story-manifest.test.mjs` holds a family's first manifest story to plain parts, with no ref, spy, element or helper of its stories file, and `test/family-status.test.mjs` holds every family page to one status line.

Every exported family, ActionBar, WorkPane and Inspector included, has stories and a page, so the render, accessibility and layout checks reach all of them.

Keep one family page with useful examples, generated props and relevant usage/accessibility guidance. The props tables come from the types: a part's own props and the Base UI props it inherits (a Dialog's `open` and `onOpenChange`), not the DOM's own attributes. There is no required heading set. Omit sections that add no information, and review the prose against the current examples and implementation. What an earlier spelling is written as now goes on [Upgrading](?path=/docs/guidance-upgrading--docs), under the family's name, and the changelog entry for the rename links it.

The package runs its stories through three scripts, from the repository root:

```sh
npm run test:a11y -w packages/design-system
npm run test:layout -w packages/design-system
npm run test:gates -w packages/design-system
# one file through both layout checks, from inside packages/design-system
npx vitest run --project storybook-narrow --project storybook-contained src/stories/components/Badge.stories.tsx
```

`test:a11y` runs every story in light, dark and forced-colours Chromium using Storybook’s built-in `test` tag. Each story gets a render check; its `play` function adds interaction assertions. Axe runs alongside them, and a story fails on a console error or on a Base UI or React warning. Dark mode also checks reduced motion. Two gates ride on these runs: in light, every tab stop is focused in turn and fails when a clipping or scrolling ancestor cuts half or more of its ring; in forced colours, a selected, pressed, current or checked item fails when it looks the same as its unselected sibling once system colours replace the tokens.

`test:gates` runs four more projects, without axe: `storybook-touch`, every story on a 390px touch phone with a coarse pointer and no hover, where a control under 24 by 24 CSS pixels by axe's `target-size` rule (counting the hit area `touch-target` draws) or a control that shows only on hover fails (the kit's one touch predicate is `any-pointer: coarse`: `any-pointer-coarse:` in a class, `useTouch` in script); `storybook-short`, the overlay families in a 320 by 256 window, where a control that takes focus less than half in view, or a title nothing scrolls back to, fails; `storybook-long`, the families that show titles, values and stamps, in the 320px frame with every text 40% longer and an 80-character unbroken token added, where sideways scroll, paint past the frame or text cut with no ellipsis fails; and `storybook-rtl`, the families whose layout or keys follow the writing direction (tables, trees, tabs, toolbars, paths, timelines, fields in place, toasts, the icon rail) laid out right to left by the Direction toolbar, where a text alignment that names a physical side, anything visible past the page's right edge (its start, out of reach) or a play that fails mirrored fails. A play that measures a line's start or end, scrolls sideways or presses a sideways arrow asks `src/stories/_lib/direction.ts` (`along`, `towardsEnd`, `arrows`), so it holds either way the page reads, and `ledger/no-non-token-class` reports a class that names a physical side (`text-left`, `pl-200`, `right-0`, `border-l`, `rounded-r-large`) outside a variant that names one, with its logical twin. `test/story-gates.ts` says what each gate measures; a story that predates a gate is listed with its count in `test/gates-allow.json`, which may only shrink.

`test:layout` renders every story twice more, without axe, once its web fonts have loaded: at a 390px phone (`storybook-narrow`) and in a 320px frame on the desktop canvas (`storybook-contained`, the toolbar's Frame: 320px container). A story fails when the page scrolls sideways, a word of four or more letters breaks across two lines, or anything paints past either edge of the frame outside a scroller. At phone width, visible content past the page's left edge fails too, because no one can scroll to it. A story whose overflow is its lesson (a Don't) is listed by id, with its reason, in `test/layout-allow.json`; a fixture that overflows because of a fixed width becomes fluid instead of being listed.

Two things change how a story is measured, both visible in the story. `layout: "fullscreen"` is page-level and gets no frame, so the contained check skips it; the phone check still measures it. A story's `globals` render it at the width they pin: a phone pin is measured at that width in both checks (inside the 320px frame in the contained one), a desktop pin takes it off the phone width, and `frame: "canvas"` takes it out of the frame. Pin a width only for a play function that measures a layout existing at that width. Overlays positioned against the viewport (sheets, dialogs, toasts) are not measured for paint past an edge, but an open one's words are checked at phone width; check an overlay's fit in a render at phone width.

Keep examples and their interaction tests in the same component’s `.stories.tsx` file. Add assertions to an existing example before introducing another render fixture. Use `fn()` from `storybook/test` for callbacks instead of rendering test counters or “check refs” buttons. Add a distinct story only for a distinct useful state or workflow. The Interactions panel shows the test steps; test-only controls do not belong in the component showcase.

Storybook applies `dev`, `test` and `manifest` automatically. No custom tag is needed to opt in, and no tag opts a story into a check. `!manifest` keeps a story that renders a `_lib` helper, and every Don't, out of the manifest MCP reads ([Writing stories](?path=/docs/guidance-writing-stories--docs)). Use `!test` only for a documented case that cannot run automatically; intentional accessibility anti-examples can scope an exception to the demonstrated axe rule, with an explanation beside the story. The other accessibility checks and the render test still run. Do not recreate a separate hidden story catalog.

See [Storybook interaction tests](https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-tests/interaction-testing) and [tags](https://storybook.js.org/docs/writing-stories/tags). The package unit suite covers nonvisual logic and token generation. The packed consumer suite verifies installation, declarations, SSR and generated CSS.

Axe does not certify keyboard quality, reading order, useful labels, focus visibility, zoom or screen-reader announcements. Review representative workflows with a screen reader and Firefox/WebKit before release. Contrast results cover the declared pairs, including alpha compositing and interactive states; they do not prove every possible composition. Resting text-field borders keep the intentionally lighter 1.5:1 visibility floor, and meet 3:1 at increased contrast. The Checkbox and Radio boundary (`color.border.bold`) and the Switch's off track (`color.background.input.track`) meet 3:1 against every surface in every mode; focus and danger borders meet 3:1 against their declared adjacent surfaces. Text and non-text checks keep their separate thresholds.

## Reference workflows for review

| Workflow                     | Stories                       | Review focus                                                             |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Validate and repair a form   | Patterns/Forms stories        | All errors, first focus, preserved values, custom control wiring.        |
| Pick and submit a date       | Components/DatePicker stories | Closed picker FormData, external form, reset, disabled omission.         |
| Save inline with failure     | Patterns/Editable stories     | One pending operation, rollback ownership, external updates.             |
| Complete a nested modal task | Components/Dialog stories     | Escape, successful close, return to correct opener.                      |
| Navigate a hierarchy         | Components/Tree stories       | One tab stop, hierarchy, typeahead, selected item removal.               |
| Filter records and recover   | Patterns/DataTable stories    | Empty results, clear filters, visible labels, durable supported actions. |
| Read a chart                 | Patterns/Chart stories        | Table equivalent, deterministic formatting and color mode.               |

## Ownership and lifecycle

The repository maintainers own the package contract and review changes to tokens, accessibility behavior and adapters. A contribution names a responsible reviewer and intended consumer. A new part's page opens with `**Status: Experimental.**`, saying why and who owns it, and names its known limitations; it becomes `**Status: Stable.**` once a product screen uses it and the documented checks and consumer review pass. A deprecated part's status line names its replacement, and the changelog and [Upgrading](?path=/docs/guidance-upgrading--docs#status) give the migration. User testing and assistive-technology review remain release work even when all automated checks pass.

<!-- page: Tokens/Color (src/stories/tokens/Color.mdx) -->

# Colour and elevation

Semantic colour is tier 1. Every token references a palette step and carries a light value and a dark value, so a component never knows which mode it is in. Utilities are generated per property: a text token is only reachable as `text-*`, a background as `bg-*`, an icon as `icon-*`, a border as `border-*`. A `default` segment drops out of the name: `color.text.default` in the source is `color.text` on the sheet and `text-default` in a class.

The ramps are on the Palette sheet (Tokens/Palette). No ramp step has a utility. A component reads a semantic token or nothing.

## One accent

The canvas is white: `elevation.surface` is `color.neutral.0` in light. Blue is the only accent. Brand, selected, information and focus all draw on the blue ramp, so blue is spent on action, selection, focus and links and on nothing else.

| Job                                                          | Token                                            | Utility                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ |
| The primary button                                           | `color.background.brand.bold`                    | `bg-brand-bold`                      |
| An active row, a checked menu item, an open dropdown trigger | `color.background.selected`                      | `bg-selected`                        |
| A selected tab's text and underline                          | `color.text.selected`, `color.border.selected`   | `text-selected`, `border-selected`   |
| The focus ring                                               | `color.border.focused` at `border.width.focused` | `border-focused`, `border-w-focused` |
| A link                                                       | `color.text.brand`                               | `text-brand`, or TextLink            |

Ids and counts stay neutral, and so does an avatar by default. An Id is blue only inside a link or a button (`ledger/id-not-blue`). Colour that carries no meaning is the accent family: `color.background.accent.*` in six hues, `subtler` under `color.text.accent.*` and `bolder` under `color.text.inverse`, for an avatar's tint, fill or gradient and, later, a tag. Teal and purple reach only the accent family and `color.chart.*`; a status is never drawn in them.

## Text and icons

| Job                                                        | Text                  | Icon                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------- |
| Content, sentence-case headings, buttons                   | `color.text`          | `color.icon`          |
| Secondary: navigation, field labels, subtle links          | `color.text.subtle`   | `color.icon.subtle`   |
| Tertiary: metadata, breadcrumbs, placeholders, helper text | `color.text.subtlest` | `color.icon.subtlest` |
| Off                                                        | `color.text.disabled` | `color.icon.disabled` |
| On a bold fill                                             | `color.text.inverse`  | `color.icon.inverse`  |

An icon mirrors its text, one step bolder where a thin glyph needs it. Text and Heading take these as `color="color.text.subtle"`; a class says `text-subtle`.

## Status

A tone is one decision. The subtle fill takes the tone's text. The bold fill takes inverse text; warning's bold fill is light, so it takes `color.text.warning.inverse`. A dot takes the tone's icon colour.

| Tone          | Subtle fill                    | Text                     | Bold fill                           | Icon                     |
| ------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `neutral`     | `color.background.neutral`     | `color.text.subtle`      | `color.background.neutral.bold`     | `color.icon.subtlest`    |
| `information` | `color.background.information` | `color.text.information` | `color.background.information.bold` | `color.icon.information` |
| `success`     | `color.background.success`     | `color.text.success`     | `color.background.success.bold`     | `color.icon.success`     |
| `warning`     | `color.background.warning`     | `color.text.warning`     | `color.background.warning.bold`     | `color.icon.warning`     |
| `danger`      | `color.background.danger`      | `color.text.danger`      | `color.background.danger.bold`      | `color.icon.danger`      |

Reach these through the `tone` prop on Badge, Dot, Indicator, Alert, Progress and Stat, never by hand. The `subtler` and `subtle` emphases are for lozenges and non-interactive chips. `hovered` and `pressed` are their own tokens, never alpha on the default (`ledger/no-alpha-token`). What each tone means is on [Badge](?path=/docs/components-badge--docs); a product keeps its values, their words and their tones in one status map that follows those meanings.

## Minted, not yet drawn

The matrix is complete on purpose: every fill has `hovered` and `pressed`, every tone has `subtler`, `subtle`, the default and `bold`, the inverse subtle fill exists for a control on a bold fill, and the bolder text colours exist for a word on a tone's label. About forty of them have no part that draws them yet: a token is minted when its place in the grammar is clear and drawn when the part arrives, so a part never invents a colour. The families still open, and the part each waits for:

| Family                                                                                                       | Waits for                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `color.background.{danger,warning,success,information}.{hovered,pressed}` and `.subtler.{hovered,pressed}`   | A status fill that is pressed: a toned chip that filters, a status pill that opens its record.                                                         |
| `color.background.{warning,success,information}.bold.{hovered,pressed}`, `neutral.bold.{hovered,pressed}`    | A bold button in a tone other than brand and danger.                                                                                                   |
| `color.background.brand.boldest` and states, `brand.subtlest.{hovered,pressed}`, `selected.bold` and states  | A pressed primary, a hovered brand tint, a bold selected control.                                                                                      |
| `color.background.danger.subtler`, `warning.subtler`, the three `.subtle`                                    | A lozenge emphasis between the subtle fill and the bold one.                                                                                           |
| `color.background.inverse.subtle`                                                                            | The resting fill of a control on a bold surface; its `hovered` and `pressed` are drawn by the Banner's action.                                         |
| `color.text.{danger,warning,success,information}.bolder`, `color.border.warning`, `color.border.information` | A word on a tone's label; a 3:1 status border in those tones.                                                                                          |
| `color.icon.warning.inverse`, `color.border.inverse`                                                         | An icon and a border on a bold warning fill; the Box paints its text inverse and icons follow it, so the icon token is reached through `currentColor`. |
| `elevation.surface.pressed`, `elevation.surface.overlay.{hovered,pressed}`, `elevation.shadow.overflow`      | A pressed page surface, a hovered overlay, a scroll edge.                                                                                              |

`color.background.input.pressed` is drawn by every field on focus, and `color.background.inverse.subtle.hovered` and `.pressed` by the Banner's action under the pointer. The chart tokens are reached at runtime through `tone`, which a name scan cannot see; Patterns/Chart.

## Borders

Every border is a 1px hairline: `border.width` is 1px and `color.border` is the default colour. Prefer a rule to a box.

| Job                             | Token                   | Utility                             |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Hairlines, dividers, flat cards | `color.border`          | `border-default`                    |
| Emphasis that must pass 3:1     | `color.border.bold`     | `border-bold`                       |
| Text fields                     | `color.border.input`    | `border-input`                      |
| Checkbox and radio boxes, 3:1   | `color.border.bold`     | `border-bold`                       |
| Focus ring, 2px                 | `color.border.focused`  | `border-focused border-w-focused`   |
| Selected tab or item, 2px       | `color.border.selected` | `border-selected border-w-selected` |
| Off                             | `color.border.disabled` | `border-disabled`                   |

The text-field border is light by decision: `color.border.input` is 1.87:1 on the light page and about 2:1 on the dark one, and the contrast test holds it at 1.5:1 or more on the page, sunken, raised, overlay and input surfaces, including the hovered and pressed input fills. The input surface, the hover tint and the focus and danger borders, which do meet 3:1, carry the affordance. A choice control has no input surface and no text to carry it, so the Checkbox and Radio box is drawn in `color.border.bold` and the Switch's off track in `color.background.input.track`, each 3:1 on every surface. A reader who asks for more contrast gets a text-field boundary of 3:1 or more on every one of those surfaces too: see Increased contrast below. Decorative rules and disabled controls use separate tokens; a decorative border must not be the only visible boundary of an interactive control.

The automated contrast contract covers default, hovered and pressed text/fill pairs, selected rows (their subtle text and icons at rest, under the pointer and pressed; their meta text in `color.text.subtlest`, an Absent included, and the name link in `color.text.brand` at rest and under the pointer, a press being momentary), a highlighted menu item's count or meta line, status fills, focus and input borders, the focus ring on the fills a focused control sits inside, the accent pairs, the chart's marks, and translucent fills on their actual parent surfaces in both modes, at the standard contrast and the increased one. Alpha blends are composed in encoded sRGB before calculating WCAG luminance. These token checks complement rendered interaction and manual accessibility checks; they do not establish conformance for arbitrary custom combinations.

A status border comes in `default` (3:1) and `subtle` (decorative): `color.border.danger`, `color.border.danger.subtle`, and the same for warning, success and information.

## Increased contrast

The standard values above are the default, low-contrast choices included: a 1.87:1 field border, a 1.22:1 hairline, and selected, pressed and highlighted fills between 1.05:1 and 1.8:1. A reader who asks the system for more contrast gets a second set of values, in light and in dark, where every boundary and every state reads 3:1 against the surface, and a focus ring reads 3:1 on those states too.

| What turns it on                     | Where                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `prefers-contrast: more`             | The reader's system setting, for the whole document, unless the root pins standard.       |
| `data-contrast-mode="more"`          | Pins increased contrast on that element and everything inside it, usually `html`.         |
| `data-contrast-mode="no-preference"` | Pins the standard contrast, whatever the system says.                                     |
| No attribute                         | Follows the reader's setting, as `data-color-mode` absent follows `prefers-color-scheme`. |

The contrast and the colour mode are independent and nest either way: a dark region inside an increased-contrast page, or an increased-contrast region inside a dark one, takes the nearest of each. The mode switch does not set the contrast yet; a product that offers the choice writes the attribute on `html` itself, and the Storybook's Contrast toolbar does the same.

| Family                                                                                                    | Standard                                                                                                                            | Increased                                                                                                                                      |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Text-field boundary, `color.border.input`                                                                 | 1.87:1 light, about 2:1 dark                                                                                                        | 3:1 or more on every surface and on the hovered and pressed input fills                                                                        |
| Hairline, `color.border`                                                                                  | 1.22:1 light, about 1.3:1 dark                                                                                                      | 3:1 on every surface                                                                                                                           |
| Pressed and highlighted fills, `color.background.neutral` and `.subtle`, rest, hover, pressed             | 1.13:1 to 1.46:1 light, 1.16:1 to 1.78:1 dark                                                                                       | 3:1 against the surface they sit on                                                                                                            |
| Selected fills, `color.background.selected`, rest, hover, pressed                                         | 1.05:1 to 1.22:1 light, 1.23:1 to 1.97:1 dark                                                                                       | 3:1 against the surface                                                                                                                        |
| Text and icons on those fills: `color.text`, `.subtle`, `.selected`; `color.icon`, `.subtle`, `.selected` | 4.5:1 and 3:1 on the standard fills                                                                                                 | `color.text`, the subtle ones and the selected ones step darker in light and lighter in dark, so they keep 4.5:1 and 3:1 on the stronger fills |
| Focus ring, `color.border.focused`                                                                        | 3:1 on the surface and on the neutral and selected fills at rest, hovered and the selected press; 2.8:1 on a neutral press in light | 3:1 on the surface and on every fill above, a press included; darker in light, lighter in dark                                                 |

What it costs: secondary text reads closer to primary text (in dark, `color.text.subtle` is the same step as `color.text`), and a 3:1 fill is a mid tone, so a coloured word (a link, a status) on a hovered or selected row is not promised its 4.5:1 there, nor a coloured boundary (`color.border.selected`, `color.border.danger`) its 3:1 against the fill; each keeps 3:1 against the surface. `color.text.subtlest` steps up too but is held to the surfaces alone, not to the stronger fills, so a placeholder still reads apart from a value. Every pairing on this page is tested at both contrasts: `test/contrast.test.mjs` runs light and dark at each.

Nothing reads the contrast directly: a part uses the tokens and follows. `tokenValue()` returns the value in effect at the element it is given. For Figma and other DTCG tools the package exports `tokens.dtcg.light-contrast.json` and `tokens.dtcg.dark-contrast.json` beside the light and dark documents. Forced colours (Windows High Contrast) is a different mode, where the system replaces the palette; `forced-colors.css` handles it.

_Example: story `Stories.IncreasedContrast`._

## Blanket and skeleton

`color.blanket` (`bg-blanket`) is the scrim under a dialog, a drawer and the open side nav on a small screen. `color.skeleton` (`bg-skeleton`) is the loading fill; `color.skeleton.subtle` is its shimmer.

## Chart

A series on a chart is a `color.chart.*` token: a status tone when the series is a status, `brand` for the one the reader is asked to look at, `neutral` for context, or the categorical set, six hues in a fixed order validated for colour vision, then Other. Two scales exist for a heatmap: `sequential`, one hue from near zero to the most, and `diverging`, red against blue around grey. Every step is the same in both modes, and every series tone has a `hovered` step (one darker in light, one lighter in dark) for the mark under the pointer. `color.chart.warning.bold` is the warning orange on a grey track, a step darker than the series in light: a Progress bar's warning fill, which holds 3:1 on the track over every surface. The parts read these through `tone` on a series; `fill-chart-*`, `stroke-chart-*` and `bg-chart-*` let a bespoke SVG take the same paint. How each is used is on Patterns/Chart.

Every series tone (`brand`, `neutral`, the four statuses), the six categorical hues, Other, and each one's `hovered` step hold 3:1 against every surface a chart sits on, in both modes, so a bar, a line or a slice reads as a mark without its label. The low steps of `sequential` (1 to 3 in light, 1 in dark) and the non-bold `diverging` steps do not: they are heatmap cells, told apart from the surface by the cell's border and read by the value in them, never a mark alone.

_Example: story `Stories.Chart`._
